title: Contraception: Match the Method to the Patient
bottomLine: Contraceptive counselling is preference-sensitive care. Start with pregnancy intention, effectiveness priorities, bleeding goals, contraindications, medications, STI protection, privacy and access; do not make age, parity or disability a reason to withhold a highly effective reversible method.
recognize: Long-acting reversible contraception is highly effective and appropriate for many adolescents and adults.
Combined estrogen-containing methods require assessment for thrombotic/cardiovascular contraindications.
Progestin-only methods are often options when estrogen is unsuitable, but bleeding-pattern counselling is essential.
differentiate: Contraception prevents pregnancy; condoms/barriers also reduce STI transmission risk and may be recommended alongside another contraceptive.
Emergency contraception addresses a recent exposure; it does not provide reliable protection for later unprotected intercourse unless an ongoing method is established.
assessment: Ask pregnancy intention, last menstrual period/unprotected intercourse, migraine with aura, smoking, hypertension, VTE/thrombophilia, postpartum/breastfeeding status, medications, sexual health/STI risk and patient preference.
For adolescents, provide confidential care within applicable mature-minor/provincial rules and explain limits of confidentiality.
workup: A pelvic exam, Pap test or routine laboratory panel is not required before most contraceptive methods.
Check pregnancy status and method-specific requirements rather than delaying contraception for unrelated testing.
management: Offer the full range of medically appropriate methods using shared decision-making rather than tiered coercion.

When emergency contraception is needed, offer the most effective appropriate option available and start it as soon as possible; establish ongoing contraception and backup instructions according to the EC method used.
medicationSafety: Review enzyme-inducing drugs that can reduce effectiveness of some hormonal methods.
Avoid estrogen-containing contraception when the patient's thrombotic/cardiovascular risk makes it unsafe.
Copper IUD is a highly effective nonhormonal emergency-contraception option when appropriate.
redFlags: New focal neurologic symptoms on estrogen-containing contraception
counselling: Discuss expected bleeding changes before initiation so predictable side effects do not become avoidable discontinuation.
Use reproductive-justice language: the goal is the patient's preferred method or no method—not the clinician's preferred choice.
followUp: Most methods do not require a routine 'permission visit' to continue, but provide access for adverse effects, bleeding concerns, removal or method change.
examTrap: Refusing an IUD/implant to an adolescent or nulliparous patient solely because of age or parity.
oneLinePearl: The best contraceptive is the medically safe method the patient can and wants to use.
sourceBasis: SOGC 2025 Progestin-Only Contraception Bleeding Position Statement
Canadian Paediatric Society Contraceptive Care for Canadian Youth

title: Abnormal Uterine Bleeding: Stabilize, Then Classify
bottomLine: In abnormal uterine bleeding, first decide whether bleeding is causing hemodynamic instability or significant anemia, then exclude pregnancy and classify structural versus nonstructural causes. Do not assume every irregular cycle is hormonal.
recognize: Heavy bleeding can present with flooding, clots, fatigue, dyspnea, dizziness or iron deficiency.
Anovulatory bleeding is common in early adolescence/perimenopause, but pregnancy, coagulopathy, thyroid disease, medications and structural pathology still matter.
Postcoital or postmenopausal bleeding has a different malignancy/cervical differential.
differentiate: Pregnancy-related bleeding is not routine AUB and must be evaluated separately.
PALM-COEIN provides a useful structural/nonstructural framework, but the immediate question is stability.
assessment: Assess vitals, bleeding amount/tempo, pregnancy possibility, pelvic pain, medications/anticoagulants, bleeding history, anemia symptoms and cancer risk.
Ask adolescents about easy bruising, epistaxis and bleeding since menarche when a bleeding disorder is plausible.
workup: Pregnancy test when pregnancy is possible, CBC/ferritin for significant or chronic heavy bleeding, and targeted TSH/coagulation/other testing based on history.
Use pelvic ultrasound and endometrial assessment according to age, risk and persistent abnormal bleeding rather than routinely for every young patient.
management: Unstable hemorrhage requires emergency gynecologic/acute-care management.
Stable heavy bleeding can be treated with hormonal or nonhormonal options matched to contraindications, fertility goals and cause; correct iron deficiency.
Investigate persistent/recurrent bleeding rather than repeatedly suppressing it without diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Estrogen-containing treatment may be unsafe with VTE/high cardiovascular risk.
Tranexamic acid requires thrombosis-risk consideration and clear dosing instructions; NSAIDs are inappropriate when bleeding risk/renal/GI disease outweigh benefit.
redFlags: Rapid pad/tampon saturation with ongoing heavy flow
counselling: Ask what bleeding pattern is unacceptable to the patient; treatment success includes quality of life, not only cycle regularity.
followUp: Recheck symptoms/hemoglobin or iron stores when clinically indicated and close the loop on imaging/biopsy results.
examTrap: Starting oral contraceptives for heavy bleeding before checking pregnancy and hemodynamic/anemia severity.
oneLinePearl: AUB: stability first, pregnancy second, cause third.

title: Chlamydia, Gonorrhea, and Syphilis
bottomLine: STI care is site-specific and partner-aware. Test based on sexual practices rather than identity assumptions, treat with the current PHAC regimen, address coinfection and pregnancy, and complete partner/public-health steps required in the jurisdiction.
recognize: Chlamydia and gonorrhea are frequently asymptomatic; urethral/cervical discharge, dysuria, pelvic/testicular pain or rectal/pharyngeal symptoms can occur.
Syphilis can mimic many conditions; painless chancre, secondary rash including palms/soles, neurologic/ocular symptoms or pregnancy exposure require specific evaluation.
Extragenital infection is missed if only urine/cervical testing is done when oral/anal exposure occurred.
differentiate: NAAT is highly sensitive for chlamydia/gonorrhea, while culture becomes important for gonorrhea treatment failure/resistance and test-of-cure strategy.
A positive syphilis serology must be interpreted with treponemal/nontreponemal testing, prior treatment and clinical stage.
assessment: Take a confidential, nonjudgmental sexual history covering anatomy/sites exposed, barrier use, partners, pregnancy possibility, symptoms, previous STIs, PrEP/PEP needs and safety/coercion.
Offer HIV and other STI testing according to risk and current guidance.
workup: Collect NAAT from all relevant exposed sites; obtain gonorrhea culture when treatment failure/resistance is suspected and according to test-of-cure guidance.
Use stage-appropriate syphilis serology and urgent ophthalmic/neurologic assessment when ocular/neurosyphilis is possible.
management: PHAC's June 2026 guidance uses ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once as the preferred regimen for uncomplicated gonorrhea in adults/adolescents aged 10 years and older; add chlamydia treatment when chlamydia has not been excluded.
Treat chlamydia/syphilis according to current PHAC stage/pregnancy guidance and ensure partner management.
PHAC recommends gonorrhea test of cure for all positive sites/cases, ideally using culture plus NAAT where feasible.
medicationSafety: Doxycycline is contraindicated in pregnancy in current PHAC gonorrhea/chlamydia guidance; select pregnancy-safe therapy.
Do not use an old gonorrhea regimen from memory because resistance-driven recommendations change.
counselling: Discuss abstaining from sexual exposure until treatment/partner requirements are met, condoms/barriers, partner notification and retesting where recommended.
Offer vaccination/PrEP/PEP prevention opportunities when relevant.
followUp: Track test-of-cure/retesting and partner/public-health completion according to infection and jurisdiction.
examTrap: Testing urine only despite receptive oral/anal exposure—or treating gonorrhea with a memorized outdated regimen without checking current PHAC guidance.
oneLinePearl: STI testing follows exposure sites; treatment follows today's resistance guidance.

title: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease
bottomLine: PID is a clinical diagnosis with a low threshold for empiric treatment because delay risks infertility and chronic pelvic pain. But pregnancy, ectopic pregnancy, tubo-ovarian abscess and surgical abdominal disease must be considered before routine outpatient treatment.
recognize: Lower abdominal/pelvic pain with cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness supports PID when no better cause exists.
Fever, mucopurulent discharge, STI evidence and inflammatory markers can strengthen the diagnosis but are not required.
differentiate: Ectopic pregnancy, appendicitis, ovarian torsion/cyst complication and UTI/pyelonephritis can mimic PID.
A normal ultrasound does not exclude uncomplicated PID.
assessment: Check pregnancy, vitals/systemic toxicity, STI exposure, bleeding/discharge, severe unilateral pain and ability to tolerate oral therapy/follow-up.
Perform pelvic exam when it will alter diagnosis/management and obtain STI testing.
workup: Pregnancy test and gonorrhea/chlamydia testing; use ultrasound when abscess/torsion/ectopic or another structural diagnosis is plausible.
management: PHAC June 2026 outpatient PID guidance includes ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 14 days plus metronidazole 500 mg PO twice daily for 14 days for appropriate nonpregnant outpatients.
Hospitalize/escalate when pregnancy, surgical emergency/ectopic or tubo-ovarian abscess cannot be excluded, severe illness, inability to tolerate outpatient therapy or poor response is present.
Evaluate/treat relevant sexual partners and provide prevention counselling.
medicationSafety: Pregnancy changes antimicrobial selection and disposition; doxycycline is not appropriate.
Review allergies and interactions before prescribing the multidrug regimen.
redFlags: No clinical improvement after initial outpatient therapy
counselling: Explain that early treatment protects reproductive health even when test results are pending.
followUp: Reassess clinical improvement within the recommended short interval and review STI/partner results.
examTrap: Waiting for a positive chlamydia/gonorrhea result before treating a clinically convincing PID presentation.
oneLinePearl: PID is treated on clinical probability because delayed therapy causes preventable harm.
sourceBasis: PHAC Pelvic Inflammatory Disease Guide June 2026

title: Early Pregnancy Bleeding and Ectopic Pregnancy
bottomLine: Any early pregnancy with pain, bleeding, syncope or hemodynamic instability requires ectopic pregnancy in the differential until an intrauterine pregnancy and clinical course make it safely unlikely. Stabilize first; a single hCG value cannot locate a pregnancy.
recognize: Ectopic pregnancy may cause unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain, syncope or shock, but symptoms can be subtle.
Early pregnancy loss is common and should be managed with medically appropriate options plus compassionate, trauma-informed counselling.
differentiate: Pregnancy of unknown location requires serial clinical/hCG/ultrasound interpretation; one hCG number should not be used as a definitive 'ectopic threshold'.
Ovarian torsion, corpus luteum cyst, appendicitis and urinary disease remain alternatives.
assessment: ABCs/vitals, estimated gestation, pain/bleeding, syncope, prior ectopic/tubal surgery, fertility treatment, IUD pregnancy and Rh status according to local guidance.
Assess grief/support needs without minimizing the medical evaluation.
workup: Quantitative hCG plus transvaginal ultrasound when indicated; repeat testing depends on stability, findings and local early-pregnancy pathways.
CBC/type and screen/crossmatch when bleeding severity warrants.
management: Hemodynamic instability or suspected rupture requires immediate emergency gynecologic/surgical care.
Stable confirmed ectopic pregnancy may be managed medically or surgically according to size/hCG/fetal cardiac activity, contraindications, follow-up reliability and patient preference.
Early pregnancy loss management may be expectant, medical or procedural when clinically appropriate.
medicationSafety: Methotrexate has strict eligibility/contraindication and follow-up requirements; do not use when follow-up is unreliable or rupture is suspected.
counselling: Use clear language about uncertainty and provide exact return precautions; acknowledge pregnancy loss as significant regardless of gestational age.
followUp: Pregnancy of unknown location or medically managed ectopic requires reliable serial follow-up until resolution/location is established.
examTrap: Reassuring a bleeding pregnant patient because hCG is below a remembered discriminatory-zone number.
oneLinePearl: hCG trends pregnancy tissue; ultrasound and clinical status locate danger.

title: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy
bottomLine: New hypertension in pregnancy/postpartum is not just a blood-pressure problem: look for preeclampsia-related maternal organ dysfunction and fetal risk. Severe hypertension or neurologic, hepatic, renal, hematologic or pulmonary features require urgent obstetric assessment.
recognize: Preeclampsia may present with hypertension plus proteinuria and/or other maternal organ dysfunction; absence of edema does not exclude it.
Headache, visual symptoms, RUQ/epigastric pain, dyspnea, neurologic change or reduced fetal movement are warning symptoms.
Preeclampsia can first present postpartum.
differentiate: Chronic hypertension predates pregnancy/appears early; gestational hypertension develops later without preeclampsia features; superimposed preeclampsia can occur on chronic hypertension.
Headache in pregnancy/postpartum has a broad differential, but hypertension plus neurologic symptoms requires urgent preeclampsia evaluation.
assessment: Repeat BP correctly, assess symptoms/reflexes/volume status, fetal concerns and medication history; review prior preeclampsia and comorbid risk factors.
Do not rely on proteinuria alone to determine severity.
workup: CBC/platelets, creatinine, liver enzymes, urine protein assessment and fetal evaluation according to gestational age/severity; use local obstetric pathway.
management: Severe hypertension or preeclampsia with severe maternal/fetal features needs immediate obstetric/acute-care management.
Use pregnancy-safe antihypertensives and magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis/treatment when indicated through obstetric protocols.
Delivery timing is determined by gestational age, maternal/fetal status and severity—not by outpatient BP treatment alone.
medicationSafety: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are contraindicated during pregnancy.
Postpartum/breastfeeding medication selection differs and should be actively reconciled rather than simply stopping treatment.
counselling: Teach urgent warning symptoms and postpartum BP follow-up; explain long-term cardiovascular-risk implications after hypertensive pregnancy.
followUp: Postpartum BP surveillance and transition to primary care are essential because disease can worsen after delivery and future cardiovascular risk is increased.
examTrap: Calling postpartum severe headache 'sleep deprivation' without checking BP and preeclampsia features.
oneLinePearl: Preeclampsia is pregnancy hypertension plus maternal/fetal disease—not just protein in urine.
sourceBasis: SOGC Guideline No. 426: Hypertensive Disorders of Pregnancy

title: Febrile Infant 90 Days or Younger
bottomLine: In an infant 90 days or younger, a rectal temperature of 38.0°C or higher is fever even if the infant looks well. Age-specific invasive-bacterial-infection risk stratification determines cultures, inflammatory markers, LP, antibiotics and disposition; appearance alone is not enough.
recognize: CPS updated its national statement May 27, 2026 and defines fever in infants 90 days or younger as rectal temperature at least 38.0°C at home or in care.
UTI is the most common serious bacterial infection, but bacteremia/meningitis risk is highest in the youngest infants.
Hypothermia below 36.0°C can also signal infection and should be taken seriously.
differentiate: A documented fever at home still counts even if afebrile in clinic.
A positive viral test does not automatically eliminate bacterial-infection risk.
Recent vaccination can explain fever, but persistent fever and age still determine evaluation.
assessment: Assess appearance/ABCs immediately, birth history/prematurity, feeding, urine output, irritability/lethargy, respiratory/skin/umbilical findings and HSV risk.
Use rectal temperature as the reference standard in this age group.
workup: CPS recommends urinalysis and urine culture for all febrile infants 90 days or younger; younger age groups also require blood culture and inflammatory markers, with LP determined by age/risk/neurologic signs.
Do not use bag urine culture as the preferred diagnostic collection method.
management: Ill-appearing infants require immediate stabilization, cultures and empiric antimicrobials without delaying treatment for LP when unstable.
Well-appearing infants follow the CPS age-based pathway; low-risk discharge options require reliable follow-up and caregiver education.
medicationSafety: Empiric antimicrobial choice is age-specific and changes when meningitis or HSV is suspected; use the current pediatric pathway rather than adult antibiotic habits.
counselling: For outpatient low-risk pathways, explain that young infants can deteriorate and give specific feeding, breathing, alertness and fever return precautions.
followUp: CPS recommends clinician follow-up within 24–48 hours for infants discharged directly from ED/outpatient care.
examTrap: Sending a smiling 3-week-old home because the fever resolved and a viral swab is positive.
oneLinePearl: Under 90 days, fever is an age-stratified infection workup—not a 'looks well' diagnosis.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society: Management of Well-Appearing Febrile Young Infants ≤90 Days, updated May 2026

title: Bronchiolitis: Supportive Care Wins
bottomLine: Typical bronchiolitis in children 1–24 months is a clinical diagnosis treated with supportive care. Routine chest x-ray, viral testing, salbutamol, corticosteroids and antibiotics do not improve typical cases and can create harm.
recognize: Viral prodrome followed by tachypnea, increased work of breathing, crackles/wheeze and feeding difficulty is typical.
Young age, prematurity and cardiopulmonary/immunologic comorbidity increase risk for severe disease.
differentiate: Focal persistent findings, toxic appearance, atypical course or poor improvement raise pneumonia/foreign body/cardiac or other diagnoses.
Bronchiolitis physiology is airway edema/mucus rather than the bronchospasm pattern of established asthma.
assessment: Assess work of breathing, apnea/cyanosis, oxygenation, hydration/feeding and caregiver ability to manage at home.
workup: No routine CXR, blood tests or viral/bacterial cultures in typical bronchiolitis; investigate when diagnosis/severity/course is atypical.
management: Hydration, minimal handling, gentle nasal suction and oxygen when clinically indicated are the mainstays.
CPS does not recommend routine salbutamol, corticosteroids, antibiotics or chest physiotherapy for typical bronchiolitis.
medicationSafety: Unnecessary bronchodilators/steroids create adverse effects and may reinforce a false asthma diagnosis.
counselling: Teach nasal clearance, small frequent feeds and expected illness course; smoke/vape exposure reduction matters.
followUp: Discharge only when work of breathing/feeding are safe and caregivers understand return precautions.
examTrap: Ordering a CXR and salbutamol because the infant is wheezing in a classic bronchiolitis presentation.
oneLinePearl: Bronchiolitis is one of the best CNPLE examples of knowing when not to medicate.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Bronchiolitis Position Statement

title: Pediatric Acute Asthma
bottomLine: Treat pediatric asthma exacerbations by severity: rapid inhaled bronchodilation, early systemic corticosteroid for moderate/severe attacks, oxygen for hypoxemia and escalating therapy/transfer when response is inadequate. Discharge care must prevent the next attack, not just stop the current wheeze.
recognize: Severity is reflected by work of breathing, speech/feeding, air entry, oxygenation, mental status and response to initial therapy—not wheeze loudness alone.
A quiet/silent chest in a distressed child can represent critically low airflow.
differentiate: First-time wheeze in an infant may be bronchiolitis/foreign body rather than asthma.
Anaphylaxis with wheeze requires epinephrine, not asthma treatment alone.
assessment: Assess airway, respiratory effort, oxygen saturation, air entry, ability to speak/feed, prior ICU/intubation, medication use and trigger/adherence history.
workup: Routine CXR/labs are not needed for a typical responsive exacerbation; investigate complications/alternate diagnosis when response is poor or findings are atypical.
management: Give inhaled salbutamol promptly, add ipratropium in moderate/severe exacerbations according to pediatric emergency guidance, and give systemic corticosteroid early when indicated.
Escalate refractory severe attacks to ED/hospital-level therapy; do not delay transfer while repeatedly giving ineffective outpatient treatments.
At discharge, ensure an inhaled-corticosteroid-containing prevention plan, device/spacer technique and written action plan.
medicationSafety: Excessive salbutamol can cause tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia and lactic acidosis; worsening tachypnea after many doses is not always worsening bronchospasm.
Avoid sedatives in a child in respiratory distress.
counselling: Demonstrate spacer technique, review triggers and ensure family knows when to escalate using the action plan.
followUp: Arrange timely post-exacerbation reassessment of control, adherence, inhaler technique and controller intensity.
examTrap: Discharging after salbutamol works without prescribing/reviewing anti-inflammatory controller therapy and technique.
oneLinePearl: Rescue the attack, then fix the asthma plan that allowed it.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society: Managing an Acute Asthma Exacerbation in Children

title: Pediatric Gastroenteritis and Dehydration
bottomLine: The key pediatric gastroenteritis decision is hydration status. Use oral rehydration solution in small frequent amounts for mild/moderate dehydration when the child can drink; IV/NG escalation is for severe dehydration, shock, failed oral therapy or inability to safely hydrate.
recognize: Reduced urine, dry mucosa, decreased tears, tachycardia, prolonged capillary refill, lethargy and weight loss suggest dehydration; shock is a late severe finding.
Infants can deteriorate faster than older children.
differentiate: Bilious vomiting, focal peritonitis, bloody stool with toxicity, altered consciousness or severe abdominal distension is not routine viral gastroenteritis.
Plain water/juice is not equivalent to oral rehydration solution for clinically significant diarrheal losses.
assessment: Assess perfusion, mental status, urine output, oral intake, vomiting/diarrhea frequency, blood/bile, fever and baseline weight if known.
workup: Most uncomplicated gastroenteritis needs no labs or stool tests.
Check electrolytes/glucose/renal function when severe dehydration, altered state, prolonged illness or IV therapy makes results clinically useful.
management: Use oral rehydration solution and continue age-appropriate feeding/breastfeeding when possible.
A single oral ondansetron dose can help selected children 6 months to 12 years with vomiting and mild/moderate dehydration who fail oral rehydration in ED settings.
Treat shock with urgent IV resuscitation and acute-care transfer.
medicationSafety: Avoid routine antidiarrheal medications in young children.
Ondansetron is not a substitute for rehydration and requires caution in known QT/electrolyte risk.
counselling: Teach small frequent ORS, continuing feeds and urine/activity return precautions rather than withholding all food.
followUp: High-risk infants or children near the admission threshold need planned reassessment and confirmation that caregivers can obtain ORS/return to care.
examTrap: Telling parents to replace diarrheal losses with plain water or sports drinks instead of oral rehydration solution.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric diarrhea treatment is electrolyte-balanced fluid, not bowel-stopping medication.

title: Pediatric Head Injury: Image Selectively
bottomLine: Most pediatric head injuries are mild and do not need CT. Use GCS, mechanism, age and validated clinical decision guidance such as PECARN to decide observation versus imaging, while maintaining a lower threshold for concern in infants and possible maltreatment.
recognize: Repeated vomiting, severe/worsening headache, altered mental status, focal deficit, signs of skull fracture and concerning mechanism increase risk for clinically important TBI.
Children younger than 2 years require careful scalp/skull and behaviour assessment because symptoms may be subtle.
differentiate: Skull x-ray is not a routine substitute for CT in acute head-injury assessment.
Concussion can occur without abnormal CT; imaging looks for structural injury, not the diagnosis of concussion itself.
assessment: CPS recommends CABCD-E stabilization and Glasgow Coma Scale assessment.
Ask loss of consciousness, amnesia, vomiting, seizure, mechanism, anticoagulant/bleeding disorder and whether the history fits developmental ability.
workup: Use PECARN or an appropriate validated rule for mild TBI imaging decisions; CPS recommends no routine skull x-ray.
Observe selected symptomatic/severe-mechanism GCS-15 patients for 4–6 hours or image according to risk; deterioration mandates CT.
management: Moderate/severe TBI requires CT, monitoring and early trauma/neurosurgical system involvement.
Mild injury/concussion requires symptom-guided return to school/activity and avoidance of repeat head injury during recovery.
medicationSafety: Avoid medications that cloud neurologic monitoring when deterioration is possible; analgesia is still appropriate.
counselling: Provide explicit home observation/return precautions and a graded return-to-learn/activity plan for concussion.
followUp: Persistent post-concussion symptoms or academic/functional impairment need reassessment and targeted supports.
examTrap: CT-scanning every child who vomits once after a minor injury—or using a normal CT to say the child cannot have concussion.
oneLinePearl: Pediatric CT is a risk decision, not a reflex.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society: Management of the Paediatric Patient with Acute Head Trauma, 2025

title: Child Maltreatment: Recognize, Protect, Document
bottomLine: The clinician does not need to prove maltreatment before acting on reasonable concern. Stabilize injuries, obtain a careful non-leading history, document objectively, use age/injury-specific medical evaluation and follow mandatory child-protection reporting law in the province or territory.
recognize: Unexplained bruising in a nonmobile infant is a sentinel finding requiring evaluation.

Injury incompatible with developmental ability, patterned injury, multiple injury ages, concerning delay in care or changing/inconsistent history raises concern but no single feature alone proves abuse.
Sexual-abuse exams can be normal even when abuse occurred.
differentiate: Medical mimics such as bleeding disorders, bone disease and accidental injury must be considered without using them to delay protection when concern remains.
Use the Canadian term traumatic head injury due to child maltreatment (THI-CM) rather than relying on a mechanism label as a diagnosis.
assessment: Treat acute medical needs first; separately document caregiver history and the child's words verbatim when possible without repeated probing.
Perform a complete skin/oral/neurologic and injury-focused exam with trauma-informed consent/assent appropriate to age.
workup: CPS recommends a skeletal survey in suspected physical abuse in children under 2 years; additional imaging/labs/ophthalmology depend on injury pattern and child-maltreatment expertise.
Suspected sexual abuse requires timing-appropriate forensic/STI evaluation by trained services when available.
management: Report reasonable suspicion according to provincial/territorial mandatory-reporting law and ensure immediate safety before discharge.
Consult child-maltreatment pediatrics/forensic services when available; do not conduct repeated detailed investigative interviews.
medicationSafety: Provide indicated pain treatment and prophylaxis without allowing forensic concerns to delay necessary medical care.
redFlags: Threat of return to an unsafe environment
counselling: Use neutral, non-accusatory language; explain that reporting initiates a safety assessment and is not the clinician declaring guilt.
followUp: Close the loop with child-protection/medical specialty follow-up and document exactly what was reported, to whom and when.
examTrap: Waiting for definitive proof or caregiver confession before making a required child-protection report.
oneLinePearl: Reasonable concern triggers protection; proof is not the NP's threshold for reporting.
sourceBasis: Canadian Paediatric Society Child Maltreatment Guidance
CPS Suspected Sexual Abuse Guidance reaffirmed 2026
